{
  "analysis": "The training data reveals a consistent pattern of German legal organizations, specifically courts (Bundesfinanzgericht, Verwaltungsgerichtshof), tax authorities (Finanzamt, Magistrat der Stadt Wien), and companies (GmbH). The primary challenge is distinguishing these from common nouns or other capitalized words, which is solved by anchoring to specific legal context words like 'das', 'des', 'an den', or suffixes like 'GmbH'.",
  "strategy": "Create specific regex rules for the most frequent organization types found in the training data, using context anchors (preceding articles/prepositions) to ensure high precision and avoid false positives on common nouns.",
  "note": "Every rule includes output_template and output_key. Patterns use context anchors to disambiguate from non-entity capitalized nouns.",
  "rules": [
    {
      "name": "Federal Tax Court",
      "description": "Matches 'Bundesfinanzgericht' and its abbreviation 'BFG' when preceded by 'das' or 'des'.",
      "format": "regex",
      "pattern": "(?:das|des)\\s+(?:Bundesfinanzgericht(?:\\s*\\(BFG\\))?|BFG)\\b",
      "output_template": {
        "text": "$1",
        "start": "$start",
        "end": "$end",
        "type": "organisation"
      },
      "output_key": "entities",
      "priority": 10,
      "reasoning": "High frequency entity in legal texts; context 'das/des' ensures it's the court, not a generic noun."
    },
    {
      "name": "Administrative Court",
      "description": "Matches 'Verwaltungsgerichtshof' when preceded by 'an den' or 'des'.",
      "format": "regex",
      "pattern": "(?:an\\s+den|des)\\s+Verwaltungsgerichtshof(?:es)?\\b",
      "output_template": {
        "text": "$1",
        "start": "$start",
        "end": "$end",
        "type": "organisation"
      },
      "output_key": "entities",
      "priority": 9,
      "reasoning": "Specific court name; context 'an den' (to the) or 'des' (of the) distinguishes it from other uses."
    },
    {
      "name": "Tax Office General",
      "description": "Matches 'Finanzamt' when preceded by 'das', 'des', or 'dem'.",
      "format": "regex",
      "pattern": "(?:das|des|dem)\\s+Finanzamt(?:es)?\\b",
      "output_template": {
        "text": "$1",
        "start": "$start",
        "end": "$end",
        "type": "organisation"
      },
      "output_key": "entities",
      "priority": 8,
      "reasoning": "'Finanzamt' is a common noun but in legal texts usually refers to the tax authority; articles confirm entity status."
    },
    {
      "name": "Vienna City Magistrate",
      "description": "Matches 'Magistrat der Stadt Wien' or 'Magistrats der Stadt Wien'.",
      "format": "regex",
      "pattern": "(?:Magistrat|Magistrats)\\s+der\\s+Stadt\\s+Wien\\b",
      "output_template": {
        "text": "$0",
        "start": "$start",
        "end": "$end",
        "type": "organisation"
      },
      "output_key": "entities",
      "priority": 7,
      "reasoning": "Specific multi-word entity for Vienna's administration; exact phrase matching prevents partial matches."
    },
    {
      "name": "Specific Tax Office Location",
      "description": "Matches specific tax office names like 'FA Schwechat Gerasdorf' or 'Finanzamtes Österreich'.",
      "format": "regex",
      "pattern": "(?:FA\\s+[A-Z][a-z]+\\s+[A-Z][a-z]+|Finanzamtes\\s+Österreich)\\b",
      "output_template": {
        "text": "$0",
        "start": "$start",
        "end": "$end",
        "type": "organisation"
      },
      "output_key": "entities",
      "priority": 6,
      "reasoning": "Handles specific named tax offices found in the training data that don't fit the generic pattern."
    },
    {
      "name": "Limited Liability Companies",
      "description": "Matches company names ending in 'GmbH' preceded by a name.",
      "format": "[A-Z][a-z]+(?:\\s+[A-Z][a-z]+)*\\s+GmbH\\b",
      "output_template": {
        "text": "$0",
        "start": "$start",
        "end": "$end",
        "type": "organisation"
      },
      "output_key": "entities",
      "priority": 5,
      "reasoning": "'GmbH' is a strong indicator of a company entity in German; the preceding capitalized words form the name."
    }
  ],
  "deleted_rules": []
}

WHAT MAKES A GOOD RULE:
- PRECISION OVER RECALL: A rule that matches 10 things correctly beats one that matches 100 with 20 wrong. Never sacrifice precision for recall. Missing a match is fixable later; a wrong match poisons results.
- GENERALIZE, DON'T MEMORIZE: Rules run on unseen text. Match the *structure* of values, not the exact strings you see in training data.
- USE CONTEXT: The same string can mean different things. Match surrounding words/punctuation and use capture groups ($1) to extract just the value.
- ONE RULE, ONE PATTERN: Multiple focused rules beat one giant regex. Each rule should have a clear, testable reason to exist.
- THINK ADVERSARIALLY: Before writing a rule, ask "what else could this match?" If the answer isn't empty, narrow the pattern or add context.

- \b word boundaries, (?:...) non-capturing groups, (a|b|c) alternation
- [A-Z] [a-z] \d \s character classes, +*?{n,m} quantifiers
- (?=...) lookahead, (?<=...) lookbehind — match context without consuming it
- (?i) case-insensitive flag

CAPTURE GROUPS ($1) vs FULL MATCH ($0):
- Use $0 in output_template when the entire regex match IS the value you want.
- Use $1 when you need surrounding context to disambiguate — put the value in a capture group.
  With "text": "$1", $start/$end auto-adjust to the group position automatically.

GOOD vs BAD PATTERNS (learn from these):

  BAD:  "\d+"                       — matches every number in the text, most will be wrong type
  GOOD: "(\d+)\s*(?:kg|lbs|oz)"    — only numbers followed by weight units; $1 captures the number

  GOOD: "(?:Mr|Mrs|Dr)\.?\s+([A-Z][a-z]+(?:\s+[A-Z][a-z]+)*)" — captures names after titles

  GOOD: "(?:in|from|at|near)\s+([A-Z][a-z]+(?:\s+[A-Z][a-z]+)*)" — locations after prepositions

  GOOD: "(?:email|contact)[:\s]+(\S+@\S+\.\w{2,})" — emails after a label; $1 captures address

- GENERALIZE, DON'T MEMORIZE: Rules run on unseen text. Match the *structure* of values, not the exact strings you see in training data.
- USE CONTEXT: The same string can mean different things. Match surrounding words/punctuation and use capture groups ($1) to extract just the value.
- ONE RULE, ONE PATTERN: Multiple focused rules beat one giant regex. Each rule should have a clear, testable reason to exist.
- THINK ADVERSARIALLY: Before writing a rule, ask "what else could this match?" If the answer isn't empty, narrow the pattern or add context.


- Regex patterns (for structured extraction)

REGEX SYNTAX REFERENCE:
- \b word boundaries, (?:...) non-capturing groups, (a|b|c) alternation
- [A-Z] [a-z] \d \s character classes, +*?{n,m} quantifiers
- (?=...) lookahead, (?<=...) lookbehind — match context without consuming it
- (?i) case-insensitive flag

CAPTURE GROUPS ($1) vs FULL MATCH ($0):
- Use $0 in output_template when the entire regex match IS the value you want.
- Use $1 when you need surrounding context to disambiguate — put the value in a capture group.
  With "text": "$1", $start/$end auto-adjust to the group position automatically.

GOOD vs BAD PATTERNS (learn from these):

  BAD:  "\d+"                       — matches every number in the text, most will be wrong type
  GOOD: "(\d+)\s*(?:kg|lbs|oz)"    — only numbers followed by weight units; $1 captures the number

  BAD:  "Alice|Bob|Tokyo"            — memorizes training strings, misses all unseen values
  GOOD: "(?:Mr|Mrs|Dr)\.?\s+([A-Z][a-z]+(?:\s+[A-Z][a-z]+)*)" — captures names after titles

  BAD:  "[A-Z][a-z]+"               — matches any capitalized word (way too broad)
  GOOD: "(?:in|from|at|near)\s+([A-Z][a-z]+(?:\s+[A-Z][a-z]+)*)" — locations after prepositions

  BAD:  "\b\w+@\w+\.\w+\b"         — matches email-like strings but also "user@v1.0"
  GOOD: "(?:email|contact)[:\s]+(\S+@\S+\.\w{2,})" — emails after a label; $1 captures address

  BAD:  one giant regex that handles 5 different sub-patterns
  GOOD: 5 separate rules, each handling one clear case with its own priority
